osces.title: Tuberculosis - IGRA Testing and Directly Observed Therapy Initiation
learning_objectives: Recognize clinical and radiological features of pulmonary tuberculosis
Interpret tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay results
Differentiate active TB from latent TB infection
Prescribe appropriate anti-tuberculosis therapy regimen
Explain directly observed therapy (DOT) requirements in Australia
Recognize notification requirements for TB in NSW
Counsel on infection control and contact tracing

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW (TB service consultation)

patient_demographics.name: Thuy Nguyen
patient_demographics.cultural_background: Vietnamese-Australian (migrated to Australia 2018 from Ho Chi Minh City)

scenario.presenting_complaint: Persistent cough, night sweats, and weight loss - CXR showing right upper lobe infiltrate suspicious for tuberculosis

history.hpi: Ms Nguyen presents with 8-week history of productive cough (initially dry, now producing small amounts of yellow sputum, occasional blood-streaking), drenching night sweats (requiring pajama changes 3-4 times per week), and 7kg unintentional weight loss. Also reports low-grade fevers (subjective, no thermometer readings), fatigue, and decreased appetite. No dyspnoea at rest. No chest pain. GP ordered CXR 1 week ago showing right upper lobe infiltrate with cavitation, suspicious for tuberculosis. Three sputum samples collected (AFB smears pending). Patient has history of BCG vaccination in childhood (Vietnam). No known TB contacts in Australia, but visited family in Ho Chi Minh City 10 months ago (stayed 6 weeks). Family history: Uncle in Vietnam diagnosed with TB in 2015, treated successfully.
pmhx: BCG vaccination (childhood, visible scar left upper arm)
medications: Has been taking paracetamol 1g QID for fever (self-prescribed)

social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband and 2 young children (ages 3 and 5 years) in 2-bedroom unit in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Works as chef in Vietnamese restaurant (5 days/week, handles food preparation), has continued working until last week
social_history.support: Husband supportive, extended family in Vietnam

history.family_history: Uncle had pulmonary TB 2015 (Vietnam, treated successfully), father has diabetes, mother hypertensive, children healthy

examination_findings.general: Thin young female, appears unwell, comfortable at rest

respiratory.auscultation: Reduced breath sounds right upper zone, scattered coarse crackles right upper zone, no wheeze

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema
examination_findings.lymph_nodes: No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy
examination_findings.other: BCG scar left upper arm, no clubbing, no cyanosis, no rash

chest_xray.findings: Right upper lobe heterogeneous opacity with areas of cavitation (largest cavity ~2cm diameter), patchy infiltrates right upper lobe, no pleural effusion, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy visible on plain film, left lung clear

ct_chest.findings: Right upper lobe consolidation with central cavitation (2.3cm cavity), tree-in-bud opacities right upper lobe (bronchogenic spread), small centrilobular nodules bilateral upper lobes, right hilar lymphadenopathy (nodes up to 1.5cm), no pleural effusion. Appearances highly suggestive of active pulmonary tuberculosis.

sputum_afb_smears.date: 1 week ago (3 early morning samples collected by GP)
sputum_afb_smears.specimen_1: AFB 2+ (moderate number of acid-fast bacilli seen - indicates high bacterial load)
sputum_afb_smears.culture: Pending (Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture requires 4-6 weeks), gene Xpert MTB/RIF ordered (rapid PCR test)
sputum_afb_smears.interpretation: Multiple positive AFB smears - presumptive diagnosis active pulmonary tuberculosis, patient highly infectious

genexpert_mtb_rif.result: Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex DETECTED, Rifampicin resistance NOT DETECTED
genexpert_mtb_rif.interpretation: Confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis, sensitive to rifampicin (suggests drug-sensitive TB, but full sensitivities pending culture)

interferon_gamma_release_assay.result: POSITIVE (TB antigen response 5.8 IU/mL, cut-off >0.35 IU/mL)
interferon_gamma_release_assay.interpretation: Indicates Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection (cannot differentiate active from latent TB, clinical/radiological correlation required)

tuberculin_skin_test.date: Not performed (IGRA preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals, TST has false-positive risk)

hiv_serology.date: 1 week ago (routine in all TB cases)

liver_function_tests.interpretation: Normal baseline liver function (important - anti-TB drugs are hepatotoxic)

visual_acuity.color_vision: Normal Ishihara plates (important - ethambutol can cause optic neuritis)

tasks.description: Interpret investigation results to confirm diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis
Prescribe appropriate first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (RIPE regimen)
Explain directly observed therapy (DOT) requirements and rationale for intensive phase monitoring
Counsel on infection control measures and arrange respiratory isolation/contact tracing
Discuss notification requirements, monitoring for drug toxicity, and treatment duration

marking_criteria.criterion: Confirms diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis based on: Clinical features (cough, night sweats, weight loss) + CXR/CT (cavitation, tree-in-bud) + AFB smears positive + GeneXpert MTB/RIF positive
Recognizes AFB 2+ on sputum smears indicates high bacterial load and patient is highly infectious (respiratory isolation required)
Interprets GeneXpert result: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance NOT detected (drug-sensitive TB likely, start standard RIPE regimen)
Explains IGRA positive confirms TB infection but cannot differentiate active from latent (requires clinical/radiological correlation)
Prescribes first-line anti-TB therapy (RIPE regimen): Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol

Specifies correct dosing for 48kg patient (weight-based dosing critical): Rifampicin 450mg daily (10mg/kg, max 600mg), Isoniazid 300mg daily (5mg/kg, max 300mg), Pyrazinamide 1000mg daily (~25mg/kg, 20-30mg/kg range), Ethambutol 800mg daily (~15mg/kg, 15-20mg/kg range)
States intensive phase duration: 2 months (RIPE all 4 drugs), followed by continuation phase 4 months (RI only)
Prescribes pyridoxine (vitamin B6) 25mg daily with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy
Explains directly observed therapy (DOT) requirement: TB nurse/healthcare worker observes patient swallow medications 5 days/week during intensive phase
Justifies DOT: Ensures adherence, prevents drug resistance, monitors for side effects, early detection of treatment failure
Arranges respiratory isolation until sputum smears negative (usually 2 weeks of treatment, requires 3 consecutive negative AFB smears)
Advises patient to avoid public places, wear mask if must leave isolation, cover mouth when coughing (respiratory droplet precautions)
Initiates contact tracing: Household contacts (husband, 2 children ages 3 and 5), workplace contacts (restaurant staff), TB service coordinates
Explains children <5 years are high-risk contacts - require urgent IGRA testing and clinical assessment (may require prophylactic isoniazid if exposed)
States TB is notifiable disease in NSW - Public Health Unit notification mandatory within 5 days of diagnosis (doctor's responsibility)
Arranges baseline monitoring: LFTs, FBC, creatinine, visual acuity (already done), uric acid (pyrazinamide can cause gout)
Plans monitoring schedule: LFTs fortnightly for first 2 months (hepatotoxicity risk - rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide), monthly visual acuity (ethambutol optic neuritis)

Counsels on drug side effects: Hepatotoxicity (nausea, jaundice, abdominal pain → stop drugs immediately, urgent LFTs), orange urine/tears (rifampicin - harmless but warn about contact lens staining), visual changes (ethambutol → urgent ophthalmology)
Advises patient to avoid alcohol during treatment (increases hepatotoxicity risk)
Discusses total treatment duration: 6 months if drug-sensitive TB with clinical response (2 months RIPE, 4 months RI)
Arranges follow-up: Weekly during intensive phase (DOT + clinical assessment), monthly during continuation phase, repeat CXR at 2 months and end of treatment
Communicates empathetically, addresses cultural considerations (language barriers, stigma in some communities), reassures TB is curable with adherence
Safety-netting: Advises patient to seek immediate medical attention if: Severe nausea/vomiting, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain (hepatotoxicity), visual changes (optic neuritis), rash

osces.clinical_context: Tuberculosis remains a significant public health issue in Australia, with 1,300 notifications annually (incidence 5.3 per 100,000). Over 90% of cases occur in overseas-born individuals from high-TB-burden countries (South-East Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Western Pacific). Active pulmonary TB diagnosis requires: clinical features + CXR abnormalities + microbiological confirmation (AFB smears, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, culture). GeneXpert provides result within 2 hours and detects rifampicin resistance (marker for MDR-TB). Standard treatment for drug-sensitive TB is RIPE regimen: 2 months intensive phase (Rifampicin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol) + 4 months continuation phase (Rifampicin, Isoniazid). Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) is recommended in Australia to ensure adherence and prevent drug resistance. TB is notifiable in all Australian states. Contact tracing focuses on household and close contacts, especially children <5 years and immunocompromised individuals.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to TB diagnosis (integrating clinical, radiological, and microbiological data). Strong candidates will correctly prescribe weight-based dosing of RIPE regimen and add pyridoxine for neuropathy prevention. Evaluate understanding of DOT rationale (adherence, resistance prevention) and implementation. Candidates must recognize respiratory isolation requirements (AFB-positive sputum) and high-priority contact tracing (children <5 years). Assess knowledge of notification requirements (mandatory reporting to Public Health Unit within 5 days in NSW). Strong candidates will outline comprehensive monitoring schedule (LFTs fortnightly, visual acuity monthly) and counsel on serious side effects (hepatotoxicity, optic neuritis). Communication skills critical - addressing stigma, language barriers, and emphasizing curability with adherence.

red_flags.flag: Drug-induced hepatotoxicity (ALT >3x ULN with symptoms or >5x ULN asymptomatic)
red_flags.action: STOP all anti-TB drugs immediately, urgent hepatology consult, reintroduce drugs sequentially after LFTs normalize (challenge testing to identify culprit)

red_flags.flag: Ethambutol-induced optic neuritis (decreased visual acuity, red-green color blindness, central scotoma)
red_flags.action: STOP ethambutol immediately, urgent ophthalmology referral, may be irreversible if continued

red_flags.flag: Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB: resistant to rifampicin AND isoniazid) detected on GeneXpert or culture
red_flags.action: Isolate patient (negative pressure room if possible), infectious diseases specialist referral, second-line TB drugs (moxifloxacin, linezolid, bedaquiline, etc.), treatment duration 18-24 months

red_flags.flag: TB meningitis or miliary TB (disseminated TB)
red_flags.action: Hospital admission, add corticosteroids (dexamethasone), extend treatment to 12 months, neuroimaging, lumbar puncture

red_flags.flag: Pregnancy during TB treatment
red_flags.action: Continue treatment (untreated TB worse risk than drugs), AVOID pyrazinamide in first trimester if possible, rifampicin reduces OCP efficacy (barrier contraception), pyridoxine dose increase to 50mg daily

differential_diagnosis: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed diagnosis - AFB-positive sputum, GeneXpert MTB positive, cavitary CXR)
key_references: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic (eTG complete), Tuberculosis section
NSW Health Tuberculosis Guidelines 2022
Australian Mycobacterium Reference Laboratory (AMRL) - GeneXpert interpretation guidelines
WHO Treatment Guidelines for Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis and Patient Care (2017 update)

Nahid P et al. Official American Thoracic Society/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis. Clin Infect Dis 2016; 63(7):e147-e195
PBS Authority prescriptions for anti-tuberculosis medications (S100 program)

osces.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome - Berlin Criteria and Ventilation Strategy
learning_objectives: Apply Berlin criteria to diagnose and classify ARDS severity
Recognize precipitants and pathophysiology of ARDS
Prescribe evidence-based mechanical ventilation strategy (lung-protective ventilation)
Calculate PaO2/FiO2 ratio and interpret severity
Manage fluid balance and supportive care in ARDS
Recognize indications for prone positioning and ECMO
Identify complications of mechanical ventilation

scenario.setting: Intensive Care Unit, Young District Hospital, NSW (retrieval team en route from tertiary ICU)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Severe hypoxemic respiratory failure secondary to bilateral pneumonia - intubated and ventilated 6 hours ago

history.hpi: Mr O'Brien presented to ED 8 hours ago with 4-day history of progressive dyspnoea, productive cough (purulent sputum), fever (39.2°C at home), and rigors. Initially managed with supplemental oxygen via Hudson mask (FiO2 0.6) but developed worsening hypoxemia (SpO2 85%) and respiratory distress despite maximal oxygen therapy. CXR showed bilateral infiltrates. Intubated 6 hours ago for severe hypoxemic respiratory failure. Current ventilator settings: Assist-Control mode, TV 500mL (8mL/kg IBW), RR 20, PEEP 8 cmH2O, FiO2 0.8. Latest ABG shows PaO2 68mmHg on FiO2 0.8 (PaO2/FiO2 ratio 85 - severe ARDS). No improvement with recruitment maneuvers. Background: Previously well apart from hypertension. Non-smoker. Lives on farm with wife.

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 standard drinks per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife on farm property near Young
social_history.occupation_details: Sheep farmer, no occupational lung exposures identified

examination_findings.general: Intubated and mechanically ventilated, sedated (RASS -3), appears critically unwell

vital_signs.bp: 92/58 mmHg (MAP 69 mmHg - borderline, on 500mL fluid bolus)
vital_signs.spo2: 89% on FiO2 0.8 (severe hypoxemia despite high FiO2)

respiratory.inspection: Intubated (oral ETT 8.0mm, secured 22cm at lips), bilateral chest rise symmetrical but reduced, no pneumothorax clinically
respiratory.auscultation: Coarse crackles bilateral lung fields, equal air entry (bronchial breath sounds both sides)

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardic, MAP 69mmHg (adequate for perfusion but borderline), JVP not visible (flat - suggests hypovolemia), peripheral pulses present, cool peripheries (poor perfusion), capillary refill 3 seconds
examination_findings.other: Sedated, pupils equal and reactive, no rash, no peripheral edema, urinary catheter draining concentrated urine (oliguria - 20mL/hr last hour)

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral diffuse airspace opacification (ground-glass and consolidation), no significant pleural effusions, ETT 3cm above carina (good position), no pneumothorax, cardiac size normal, consistent with ARDS

ct_chest.date: Not yet performed (patient too unstable for transfer to CT scanner)
ct_chest.planned: Once stabilized - to assess for complications (pneumothorax, barotrauma) and rule out alternative diagnoses

renal_function.creatinine: 135 μmol/L (elevated from baseline 88 μmol/L - acute kidney injury)

sputum_culture.result_pending: Preliminary Gram stain: Gram-positive diplococci (Streptococcus pneumoniae suspected), culture pending

echocardiogram.findings: LVEF 55% (normal), no regional wall motion abnormalities, no significant valvular disease, IVC dilated (fluid overloaded), estimated PASP 38mmHg (mildly elevated)

tasks.description: Apply Berlin criteria to diagnose ARDS and classify severity
Adjust ventilator settings to lung-protective ventilation strategy (low tidal volume, appropriate PEEP)
Manage fluid balance and hemodynamic support in ARDS
Discuss adjunctive therapies (prone positioning, neuromuscular blockade) and escalation (ECMO)
Address infection source control and supportive care

marking_criteria.criterion: Applies Berlin criteria to diagnose ARDS: (1) Acute onset <1 week, (2) Bilateral opacities on CXR, (3) Not fully explained by cardiac failure (echo shows normal LVEF), (4) Hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 <300mmHg)
Calculates PaO2/FiO2 ratio correctly: 68mmHg / 0.8 = 85 mmHg
Classifies as SEVERE ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <100mmHg on PEEP ≥5 cmH2O per Berlin criteria)
Identifies precipitant: Severe bilateral pneumonia (likely Streptococcus pneumoniae based on Gram stain)
Recognizes current tidal volume 8mL/kg IBW is TOO HIGH - lung-protective ventilation requires 6mL/kg IBW (ARDSNet protocol)
Calculates correct tidal volume: IBW 62.5kg × 6mL/kg = 375mL (reduce from 500mL to 375mL)
Increases PEEP from 8 to 12-14 cmH2O (higher PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli, improves oxygenation in severe ARDS)
Maintains plateau pressure <30 cmH2O (current 32 cmH2O - reducing tidal volume will lower plateau pressure, prevents barotrauma)
Accepts permissive hypercapnia (PaCO2 48mmHg acceptable if pH >7.20) - prioritize lung protection over normocapnia
Discusses fluid management: Currently positive 2320mL in 6 hours - conservative fluid strategy reduces ARDS duration (FACTT trial)
Recommends cautious fluid resuscitation: Maintain MAP >65mmHg with vasopressors (noradrenaline) rather than excessive fluids
Addresses oliguria: Urine output 20mL/hr (oliguria) - likely pre-renal AKI from hypoperfusion, BUT avoid fluid overload (worsens ARDS)
Recommends prone positioning (16 hours daily) for severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <150mmHg) - improves survival by 50% (PROSEVA trial)
Discusses neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium infusion) for first 48 hours if PaO2/FiO2 <150mmHg - reduces ventilator dyssynchrony, improves oxygenation
States NO ROLE for corticosteroids in early ARDS secondary to pneumonia (may increase mortality per DEXA-ARDS trial)
Recognizes indications for ECMO referral: Severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <80mmHg) refractory to optimized ventilation and prone positioning
Contacts tertiary ICU retrieval team for ECMO consideration (patient has PaO2/FiO2 85, already meets ECMO criteria if no improvement)
Continues appropriate antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin for severe CAP (covers Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals)
Addresses source control: Pneumonia is source - no surgical intervention required, optimize antibiotics
Implements VTE prophylaxis (LMWH or mechanical prophylaxis if contraindicated)
Implements stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI IV)
Plans daily sedation interruption/lightening (reduces ICU length of stay, improves outcomes)
Communicates with family: Explains ARDS diagnosis, severity, treatment plan, guarded prognosis (severe ARDS mortality ~40%)

osces.clinical_context: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a severe inflammatory lung injury characterized by diffuse alveolar damage, pulmonary edema, and hypoxemic respiratory failure. Berlin criteria (2012) define ARDS by timing (<1 week), bilateral CXR opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300mmHg on PEEP ≥5, and absence of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Severity: Mild (200-300), Moderate (100-200), Severe (<100). Mortality: Mild 27%, Moderate 32%, Severe 45%. Lung-protective ventilation (ARDSNet protocol) is cornerstone: tidal volume 6mL/kg IBW, plateau pressure <30cmH2O. Adjuncts for severe ARDS: prone positioning 16hrs/day (PROSEVA trial: 50% mortality reduction), neuromuscular blockade first 48hrs (ACURASYS trial), conservative fluid strategy (FACTT trial). ECMO reserved for refractory severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 <80mmHg despite optimization).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic application of Berlin criteria and ARDS severity classification. Strong candidates will identify current ventilation as NON-protective (TV 8mL/kg, needs reduction to 6mL/kg) and adjust settings appropriately (reduce TV to 375mL, increase PEEP to 12-14cmH2O, accept permissive hypercapnia). Evaluate understanding of conservative fluid strategy (avoid excessive fluids despite oliguria, use vasopressors for MAP target). Candidates should recognize severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 85) mandates prone positioning and consideration of neuromuscular blockade. Strong candidates will identify ECMO referral criteria met and contact retrieval team. Assess ability to balance competing priorities (lung protection vs adequate oxygenation, fluid resuscitation vs ARDS worsening). Communication skills critical - explaining complex critical illness to family with realistic prognostication.

red_flags.flag: Pneumothorax during mechanical ventilation (sudden desaturation, unilateral absent breath sounds, hypotension)
red_flags.action: URGENT needle decompression (2nd ICS midclavicular line), followed by chest tube insertion, reduce PEEP if possible

red_flags.flag: Refractory hypoxemia (PaO2 <60mmHg despite FiO2 1.0, PEEP 15, prone positioning)
red_flags.action: URGENT ECMO referral, contact tertiary ICU retrieval team, consider inhaled nitric oxide as bridge

red_flags.flag: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) - new infiltrate, purulent secretions, fever after 48 hours ventilation
red_flags.action: Bronchoscopy with BAL, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem + vancomycin), de-escalate based on cultures

red_flags.flag: Auto-PEEP/breath-stacking (dynamic hyperinflation causing hypotension)
red_flags.action: Disconnect ventilator briefly to allow exhalation, reduce respiratory rate, increase expiratory time, consider sedation/paralysis

differential_diagnosis: ARDS secondary to severe bilateral pneumonia (confirmed diagnosis - Berlin criteria met, PaO2/FiO2 85)
key_references: ARDS Definition Task Force. Acute respiratory distress syndrome: the Berlin Definition. JAMA 2012; 307(23):2526-2533
ARDSNet (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Network). Ventilation with lower tidal volumes as compared with traditional tidal volumes for acute lung injury and ARDS. N Engl J Med 2000; 342:1301-1308
Guérin C et al. Prone positioning in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSEVA trial). N Engl J Med 2013; 368:2159-2168
Papazian L et al. Neuromuscular blockers in early acute respiratory distress syndrome (ACURASYS trial). N Engl J Med 2010; 363:1107-1116
National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute ARDS Clinical Trials Network. Comparison of two fluid-management strategies in acute lung injury (FACTT trial). N Engl J Med 2006; 354:2564-2575

Fan E et al. An Official American Thoracic Society/European Society of Intensive Care Medicine/Society of Critical Care Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline: Mechanical Ventilation in Adult Patients with ARDS. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2017; 195(9):1253-1263

osces.title: Chronic Cough - Differential Diagnosis and Systematic Investigation
learning_objectives: Apply systematic approach to chronic cough (>8 weeks duration)
Identify common causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, GORD, ACE-inhibitor
Recognize less common causes: bronchiectasis, ILD, lung cancer, pertussis
Formulate investigation plan based on clinical features
Interpret spirometry with bronchodilator challenge for cough-variant asthma
Prescribe empiric trials for upper airway cough syndrome and GORD
Recognize red flags requiring urgent investigation

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Persistent dry cough for 4 months - no response to multiple courses of antibiotics

history.hpi: Ms Williams presents with 4-month history of persistent dry cough. Cough is worse at night (disrupts sleep), and with talking/laughing (interferes with teaching). No sputum production. No haemoptysis. No dyspnoea at rest or on exertion. No chest pain. No wheeze. Denies fever, night sweats, or weight loss. GP has prescribed 3 courses of antibiotics (amoxicillin, doxycycline, azithromycin) with no improvement. CXR 6 weeks ago normal. Patient increasingly frustrated - cough affecting work (students comment on it), causing embarrassment. No recent viral illness preceding cough onset. Reports postnasal drip sensation and frequent throat clearing. Denies heartburn but does report occasional regurgitation of food (especially when bending over).
pmhx: Hypertension (diagnosed 6 months ago, commenced on perindopril 4mg daily)
Allergic rhinitis (seasonal, worse spring/summer, uses cetirizine PRN)

medications.name: Perindopril arginine
medications.frequency: Daily (started 6 months ago - TEMPORAL RELATIONSHIP TO COUGH)

social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 glasses wine per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband and two teenage children in Young
social_history.occupation_details: Primary school teacher (Year 3) for 20 years, exposed to childhood respiratory infections, no occupational irritants

history.family_history: Mother has asthma, father has GORD, no family history of lung cancer or ILD

examination_findings.general: Well-appearing middle-aged female, comfortable at rest, frequent throat clearing during consultation

ent_examination.oropharynx: Mild posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning (suggestive of postnasal drip)

respiratory.auscultation: Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally, no wheeze, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

chest_xray.findings: Clear lung fields, normal cardiac size, no masses or infiltrates, no pleural effusion

spirometry_with_bronchodilator_challenge.interpretation: Normal spirometry, no reversible airflow obstruction

peak_expiratory_flow_variability.date: Not performed (could be arranged for 2-week home monitoring if asthma suspected)

full_blood_count.eosinophils: 0.3 × 10⁹/L (normal, not elevated - argues against eosinophilic asthma)

tasks.description: Take focused history to identify potential causes of chronic cough and recognize medication temporal relationship
Formulate differential diagnosis prioritized by clinical features
Interpret spirometry and explain why asthma is unlikely (but not excluded)
Prescribe empiric treatment trial and arrange further investigations as needed
Provide patient education and follow-up plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies temporal relationship: Cough started AFTER perindopril commenced 6 months ago (cough onset 4 months ago = 2 months after perindopril)
Asks specifically about ACE-inhibitor cough characteristics (dry, irritating, worse at night, no sputum)
Asks about upper airway symptoms: Postnasal drip (present), throat clearing (present), nasal congestion (allergic rhinitis)
Asks about GORD symptoms: Heartburn (absent), regurgitation (present), cough worse lying down/after meals
Asks about asthma symptoms: Wheeze (absent), dyspnoea (absent), nocturnal waking (cough only, no wheeze), triggers (talking/laughing)

Formulates differential diagnosis: (1) ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (most likely), (2) Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS/postnasal drip), (3) GORD, (4) Cough-variant asthma (less likely - normal spirometry)
Recognizes ACE-inhibitor cough occurs in 10-20% of patients, mechanism: bradykinin accumulation (ACE breaks down bradykinin)
Interprets spirometry: Normal FEV1/FVC ratio (0.82), no reversibility post-bronchodilator (+0.7%, not significant) - argues against classic asthma
States normal spirometry does NOT exclude cough-variant asthma (may have normal baseline spirometry, requires bronchial provocation testing if suspected)
Prescribes intervention #1: STOP perindopril, switch to alternative antihypertensive (angiotensin receptor blocker does NOT cause cough - e.g., irbesartan 150mg daily)
Explains ACE-inhibitor cough may take 1-4 weeks to resolve after cessation (bradykinin levels normalize)
Prescribes intervention #2: Empiric trial for UACS - intranasal corticosteroid (e.g., mometasone furoate 2 sprays each nostril daily, PBS code 8455N) for 4 weeks
Prescribes intervention #3: Empiric trial for GORD - PPI (e.g., esomeprazole 40mg mane, PBS code 8849C) for 8 weeks (GORD-related cough requires higher dose, longer duration)
Justifies empiric trials: Chronic cough often has multiple contributing factors (UACS + GORD common), treating all simultaneously is standard approach
Arranges follow-up in 4 weeks to assess response to ACE-inhibitor cessation + empiric trials

Plans further investigations IF no improvement: (1) 2-week peak flow diary (assess for asthma variability), (2) Methacholine challenge test (bronchial hyper-reactivity), (3) CT chest (exclude bronchiectasis, ILD), (4) Laryngoscopy (vocal cord dysfunction)
Advises lifestyle modifications for GORD: Avoid late meals, elevate head of bed, avoid triggers (coffee, alcohol, chocolate)
Reassures patient: Normal CXR and spirometry exclude serious pathology (lung cancer, ILD), chronic cough is common and usually treatable
Discusses cough suppressants: Generally NOT recommended (don't address underlying cause), codeine linctus only if cough severely affecting sleep and all other measures failed
Safety-netting: Advises patient to return immediately if develops haemoptysis, weight loss, dyspnoea, or chest pain
Communicates clearly and empathetically, acknowledges patient's frustration (4 months of cough, multiple failed antibiotic courses)

osces.clinical_context: Chronic cough (>8 weeks duration) affects 10-20% of adults and is one of the most common reasons for respiratory clinic referral. In non-smokers with normal CXR, the three most common causes are: (1) Upper airway cough syndrome (UACS, formerly postnasal drip syndrome) - 40%, (2) Asthma/cough-variant asthma - 25%, (3) GORD - 20%. ACE-inhibitor cough occurs in 10-20% of patients (more common in females), typically develops 1 week to 6 months after starting medication, and resolves within 1-4 weeks of cessation. ARBs do NOT cause cough. Systematic approach: History → CXR → Spirometry → Empiric trials (treat UACS, GORD, asthma simultaneously) → Specialist investigations if no response (CT chest, methacholine challenge, laryngoscopy, 24hr pH impedance).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to chronic cough. Strong candidates will identify temporal relationship between perindopril and cough onset (KEY diagnostic clue - cough started 2 months after ACE-inhibitor). Evaluate ability to formulate prioritized differential diagnosis integrating history (postnasal drip, regurgitation) and investigations (normal spirometry). Candidates should recognize ACE-inhibitor cough as most likely and prescribe appropriate switch to ARB. Assess understanding of empiric trial approach for chronic cough (UACS, GORD, asthma treated simultaneously - don't wait for one trial to fail before starting next). Strong candidates will explain when to pursue further investigations (if no response to empiric trials) and recognize role of specialist tests (methacholine challenge, 24hr pH monitoring). Communication skills important - managing patient expectations (may take 4-8 weeks for improvement, cough often multifactorial).

red_flags.flag: Haemoptysis (ANY amount in chronic cough)
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest, bronchoscopy, exclude lung cancer, bronchiectasis, TB

red_flags.flag: Unintentional weight loss (>5kg) or anorexia with chronic cough
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest, exclude malignancy, TB, ILD

red_flags.flag: Chronic cough in current/ex-smoker (>10 pack-year history)
red_flags.action: CT chest mandatory (exclude lung cancer), bronchoscopy if abnormal CT

red_flags.flag: Dyspnoea or reduced exercise tolerance with chronic cough
red_flags.action: Spirometry, CT chest, exclude ILD, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension

red_flags.flag: Systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats) with chronic cough
red_flags.action: CXR, sputum AFB smears, QuantiFERON, exclude TB, lymphoma

differential_diagnosis: ACE-inhibitor-induced cough (most likely - temporal relationship, dry cough, perindopril started 6 months ago)
Upper airway cough syndrome / postnasal drip (likely contributing - postnasal drip sensation, throat clearing, allergic rhinitis, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (possible - regurgitation present, cough worse lying down)
Cough-variant asthma (less likely - normal spirometry, no wheeze, but cannot exclude without bronchial provocation testing)
Bronchiectasis (unlikely - no sputum production, normal CXR, no history of recurrent infections)
Interstitial lung disease (unlikely - normal CXR, no dyspnoea, no crackles)
Lung cancer (very unlikely - never smoker, normal CXR, no weight loss, no haemoptysis)

osces.title: Occupational Lung Disease - Asbestosis Assessment and Compensation
learning_objectives: Obtain detailed occupational exposure history for asbestos
Recognize clinical and radiological features of asbestosis
Differentiate asbestosis from asbestos-related pleural disease
Interpret HRCT findings in asbestos-related lung disease
Assess respiratory impairment and functional impact
Understand compensation pathways in NSW (icare, Dust Diseases Tribunal)
Recognize increased risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma with asbestos exposure

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW
scenario.presenting_complaint: Progressive breathlessness over 5 years - HRCT showing interstitial changes, GP suspects asbestosis

history.hpi: Mr Anderson presents with 5-year history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, now dyspnoeic walking 50 metres on flat ground (mMRC grade 3). Associated with dry cough (no sputum, no haemoptysis). No chest pain. Reports decreased exercise tolerance - previously walked 5km daily, now struggles with 200 metres. No weight loss. No fevers or night sweats. GP ordered HRCT chest 2 weeks ago showing interstitial fibrosis and pleural plaques, suspicious for asbestos-related disease. Patient worked as carpenter and builder 1965-2005 (40 years), with extensive asbestos exposure (cutting asbestos-cement sheeting, installing asbestos insulation, demolition work). No respiratory protection used until 1980s. Now seeking assessment for compensation claim.
pmhx: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (metformin 1g BD, gliclazide MR 60mg daily, HbA1c 7.2%)
Previous myocardial infarction 2012 (PCI to LAD, on aspirin + clopidogrel until 2013)

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, 40 pack-year history (smoked 1 pack/day 1965-2005, quit 20 years ago when retired)
social_history.alcohol: Social drinker, 2-3 standard drinks per week
social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife in own home in Young (purchased 1975, house contains asbestos-cement sheeting - patient installed it himself)
social_history.occupation_details: Carpenter and builder 1965-2005 (40 years), EXTENSIVE asbestos exposure: (1) Cutting/drilling asbestos-cement sheeting (fibro sheets) for wall cladding 1965-1980s (daily exposure), (2) Installing asbestos pipe insulation (lagging) in commercial buildings 1970s-1980s, (3) Demolition work 1980s-1990s (disturbing old asbestos materials), (4) No respiratory protection until mid-1980s (disposable masks only from ~1987), (5) Work clothes washed at home by wife (secondary exposure risk). Ceased asbestos work 1990, fully retired 2005.
social_history.support: Wife (also concerned about her secondary exposure)

history.family_history: Father died age 65 (pneumoconiosis - coal miner), mother died age 82 (dementia), no family history of lung cancer or mesothelioma

examination_findings.general: Elderly male, appears well, mild dyspnoea on minimal exertion (walking to examination couch)

vital_signs.spo2: 94% on room air at rest, desaturates to 88% after walking 50 metres

respiratory.auscultation: Fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles (Velcro-like), no wheeze

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, HS dual with loud P2 (possible pulmonary hypertension), no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

findings.parenchymal: Bilateral basal and subpleural interstitial fibrosis with reticular pattern, subpleural lines, ground-glass opacification in lower lobes, no honeycombing. Pattern consistent with asbestosis (basal-predominant fibrosis in patient with documented asbestos exposure).
findings.pleural: Bilateral calcified pleural plaques (diaphragmatic and lateral chest wall), NO pleural thickening or effusion. Pleural plaques are PATHOGNOMONIC for asbestos exposure.
findings.other: No lung masses, no mediastinal lymphadenopathy

hrct_chest.conclusion: Asbestosis (bilateral basal interstitial fibrosis) + asbestos-related pleural plaques. Findings consistent with significant asbestos exposure.

chest_xray.findings: Bilateral lower zone reticular shadowing, calcified pleural plaques bilateral hemidiaphragms, no masses

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Moderate restrictive ventilatory defect with severe impairment of gas transfer. Pattern consistent with interstitial lung disease (asbestosis).

autoimmune_screen.date: Today (to exclude connective tissue disease-related ILD)

tasks.description: Obtain detailed occupational asbestos exposure history (type, duration, intensity, timing)
Interpret HRCT and PFTs to confirm diagnosis of asbestosis and assess severity
Explain asbestosis diagnosis and differentiate from other asbestos-related diseases
Discuss compensation pathways (icare NSW, Dust Diseases Tribunal) and provide documentation
Counsel on lung cancer/mesothelioma surveillance and management plan

marking_criteria.criterion: Obtains comprehensive asbestos exposure history: Type (asbestos-cement, pipe insulation), duration (1965-1990, 25 years), intensity (daily cutting/drilling, demolition), lack of respiratory protection (until 1987)
Asks about latency period: First asbestos exposure 1965, symptoms started ~2020 = 55-year latency (asbestosis typically 15-40 years post-exposure)
Asks about other asbestos-related diseases: Pleural plaques (present), pleural effusion (absent), mesothelioma symptoms (absent), lung cancer (no masses on CT)
Interprets HRCT: Bilateral basal interstitial fibrosis + pleural plaques = diagnostic of asbestosis in context of asbestos exposure
Recognizes pleural plaques are PATHOGNOMONIC for asbestos exposure (but plaques themselves are benign, do not cause symptoms)
Interprets PFTs: Restrictive pattern (FVC 62% predicted), severely reduced TLCO (42% predicted) - consistent with asbestosis severity
Confirms diagnosis: Asbestosis (documented asbestos exposure + HRCT showing basal fibrosis + restrictive PFTs + exclusion of other ILD causes)
Explains asbestosis to patient: Lung scarring (fibrosis) caused by asbestos fibers inhaled during work, progressive and irreversible
Differentiates asbestosis from pleural plaques: Plaques are benign scarring of pleura (do NOT cause breathlessness), asbestosis is lung parenchymal fibrosis (DOES cause breathlessness)
Discusses smoking as synergistic risk factor: 40 pack-year history + asbestos exposure increases lung cancer risk 50-90x (vs 5x asbestos alone, 10x smoking alone)
Explains compensation eligibility: NSW icare (formerly WorkCover) for occupational lung disease, OR Dust Diseases Tribunal for asbestos-related diseases
States Dust Diseases Tribunal is specialist NSW jurisdiction for asbestos claims (faster processing, medical assessments provided)
Provides medical report/documentation: Detailed occupational history, HRCT report, PFT results, diagnosis (asbestosis), functional impairment assessment (required for compensation claim)
Advises referral to specialist solicitor (asbestos/dust diseases) - most claimants use legal representation for complex compensation process
Discusses lung cancer surveillance: Annual low-dose CT chest screening (high-risk due to asbestos + smoking history), immediate investigation if new symptoms
Discusses mesothelioma risk: Latency 20-50 years post-exposure, annual CXR insufficient (mesothelioma often presents as pleural effusion or pleural mass), CT if new symptoms
Addresses wife's secondary asbestos exposure concern: Washing work clothes at home IS recognized exposure route, should have chest X-ray screening
Discusses management: NO cure for asbestosis, supportive care (pulmonary rehabilitation, ambulatory oxygen, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination)
Arranges pulmonary rehabilitation referral (mMRC grade 3 qualifies)
Arranges ambulatory oxygen assessment (desaturates to 85% on 6MWT, likely requires supplemental oxygen for exertion)
Discusses prognosis: Asbestosis is progressive, rate varies (some stable for years, others progress to respiratory failure), 5-year survival ~80% for mild-moderate disease
Safety-netting: Advises immediate return if: Haemoptysis (lung cancer), chest pain/shortness of breath worsening (pleural effusion/mesothelioma), unintentional weight loss
Communicates empathetically, acknowledges occupational disease context (preventable exposure, employer responsibility)

osces.clinical_context: Asbestos exposure in Australia peaked 1950s-1980s (mining, manufacturing, construction). Over 10,000 Australians die from asbestos-related diseases annually (mesothelioma, lung cancer, asbestosis). Asbestosis is diffuse pulmonary fibrosis caused by asbestos fiber inhalation, latency 15-40 years, dose-dependent (higher exposure = earlier/more severe disease). Diagnosis requires: (1) documented asbestos exposure, (2) HRCT showing basal-predominant interstitial fibrosis, (3) restrictive PFTs, (4) exclusion of other ILD causes. Pleural plaques (benign calcified pleural scarring) are pathognomonic for asbestos exposure but do NOT cause symptoms. Asbestos + smoking synergistically increase lung cancer risk (50-90x vs general population). NSW Dust Diseases Tribunal provides specialist compensation pathway (medical + financial support). No cure; management is supportive (pulmonary rehab, oxygen, vaccinations, cancer surveillance).
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's systematic approach to occupational history (type, duration, intensity, timing of asbestos exposure). Strong candidates will integrate history, HRCT (basal fibrosis + pleural plaques), and PFTs (restrictive, reduced TLCO) to confirm asbestosis diagnosis. Evaluate understanding of differentiation between asbestosis (symptomatic parenchymal fibrosis) and pleural plaques (asymptomatic pleural scarring). Candidates should recognize synergistic smoking risk (40 pack-years + asbestos = 50-90x lung cancer risk) and recommend annual low-dose CT screening. Assess knowledge of NSW-specific compensation pathways (Dust Diseases Tribunal) and ability to provide appropriate medical documentation. Strong candidates will address wife's secondary exposure concern and arrange surveillance. Communication skills critical - discussing progressive incurable disease with occupational context (preventable harm).

red_flags.flag: Pleural effusion (especially bloody) in patient with asbestos exposure
red_flags.action: URGENT investigation for malignant mesothelioma - CT chest, thoracentesis with cytology, respiratory physician/thoracic surgery referral

red_flags.flag: New lung mass or nodule in patient with asbestos exposure + smoking history
red_flags.action: URGENT CT chest with contrast, PET-CT, respiratory physician referral, likely lung cancer (asbestos + smoking synergistic)

red_flags.flag: Progressive respiratory failure in asbestosis (SpO2 <88% at rest, PaCO2 rising)
red_flags.action: Consider long-term oxygen therapy, pulmonary hypertension assessment (echo), discuss advance care planning, palliative care involvement

red_flags.flag: Round atelectasis on HRCT (can mimic lung mass)
red_flags.action: Recognize benign asbestos-related finding (pleural plaque causes adjacent lung collapse), BUT exclude malignancy with PET-CT or biopsy if atypical features

differential_diagnosis: Asbestosis (confirmed diagnosis - documented exposure + HRCT basal fibrosis + restrictive PFTs + pleural plaques)
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (excluded by asbestos exposure history and pleural plaques)
Connective tissue disease-related ILD (excluded by negative autoimmune screen, no extrapulmonary features)
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (excluded by occupational history, no relevant exposures)
key_references: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (eTG complete), Occupational Lung Disease section
Australian Mesothelioma Registry - asbestos exposure assessment and surveillance
NSW Dust Diseases Tribunal - compensation guidelines for asbestosis (www.dustdiseases.nsw.gov.au)
American Thoracic Society. Diagnosis and initial management of nonmalignant diseases related to asbestos. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2004; 170:691-715
icare NSW (formerly WorkCover NSW) - occupational lung disease compensation pathways
National Lung Screening Trial - low-dose CT screening for lung cancer in high-risk groups (asbestos exposure + smoking)

osces.title: Bronchoscopy - Indication Assessment and Informed Consent
learning_objectives: Recognize appropriate indications for bronchoscopy
Assess contraindications and relative contraindications
Explain bronchoscopy procedure to patient using lay terminology
Obtain valid informed consent including risks and complications
Discuss sedation options (conscious sedation vs general anesthesia)
Plan pre-procedure investigations and preparation
Recognize when to perform endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) vs standard bronchoscopy

scenario.setting: Respiratory outpatient clinic, Young District Hospital, NSW (procedural consent clinic)
scenario.presenting_complaint: Right upper lobe mass on CT chest - referred for bronchoscopy to obtain tissue diagnosis

history.hpi: Ms Schultz presented to GP 6 weeks ago with 3-month history of persistent cough and two episodes of haemoptysis (blood-streaked sputum, total ~10mL). CXR showed right upper lobe opacity. CT chest revealed 3.2cm spiculated mass in right upper lobe with mediastinal lymphadenopathy (right paratracheal nodes up to 2.5cm). PET-CT showed FDG-avid mass (SUVmax 9.5) and mediastinal nodes (SUVmax 7.2), suspicious for lung cancer with N2 nodal involvement. Sputum cytology non-diagnostic. Now referred for bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) for tissue diagnosis and mediastinal staging. Patient anxious about procedure, requesting detailed explanation.
pmhx: Atrial fibrillation (warfarin - target INR 2-3, currently INR 2.4)

allergies.reaction: Nausea and vomiting (intolerance, not true allergy)

social_history.smoking: Ex-smoker, 25 pack-year history (smoked 1968-2005, quit 20 years ago)
social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband in Young, adult daughter lives in Sydney
social_history.occupation_details: Librarian for 35 years (retired 10 years ago), no occupational exposures
social_history.support: Husband will accompany to procedure, daughter available if needed

history.family_history: Mother died age 70 (breast cancer), father died age 75 (stroke), no family history of lung cancer

examination_findings.general: Well-appearing elderly female, comfortable at rest, appears anxious about procedure

respiratory.auscultation: Reduced breath sounds right upper zone, no wheeze, no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Irregularly irregular pulse (AF), HS dual no murmurs, no peripheral oedema

airway_assessment.dentition: Full upper and lower dentition, some loose lower teeth (potential aspiration risk during bronchoscopy)
airway_assessment.conclusion: Low risk for difficult intubation if general anesthesia required, but loose teeth require careful bronchoscope insertion

findings.primary_mass: 3.2cm spiculated mass right upper lobe (anterior segment), abutting chest wall, no rib destruction
findings.lymph_nodes: Enlarged right paratracheal lymph nodes (station 4R, largest 2.5cm), right hilar nodes (station 10R, 1.8cm), subcarinal node (station 7, 1.2cm)
findings.metastases: No liver lesions, no adrenal masses, no bone lesions

findings.primary_mass: Right upper lobe mass SUVmax 9.5 (highly FDG-avid, consistent with malignancy)
findings.lymph_nodes: Right paratracheal (4R) SUVmax 7.2, right hilar (10R) SUVmax 6.5, subcarinal (7) SUVmax 5.8 - all pathological, suggests N2 disease

coagulation.inr: 2.4 (therapeutic for AF, but ELEVATED for procedural risk)

ecg.findings: Atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 70-85 bpm, no ST/T changes

pulmonary_function_tests.interpretation: Mild restrictive pattern, adequate respiratory reserve for bronchoscopy

tasks.description: Explain indication for bronchoscopy with EBUS (tissue diagnosis and mediastinal staging)
Explain bronchoscopy procedure step-by-step using lay terminology
Discuss risks and complications to obtain valid informed consent
Address warfarin management and plan pre-procedure preparation
Answer patient questions and provide post-procedure instructions

marking_criteria.criterion: Explains indication: Lung mass on CT requires tissue diagnosis (biopsy) to confirm if cancer and determine type (guides treatment)
Explains EBUS component: Enlarged lymph nodes in chest (mediastinum) need sampling to determine if cancer has spread (staging)
States EBUS-TBNA is minimally invasive alternative to mediastinoscopy (surgical procedure) for mediastinal staging
Explains bronchoscopy procedure: Flexible tube (diameter ~6mm) with camera passed through nose or mouth into airways (bronchi) while patient sedated
Describes sedation: Conscious sedation (midazolam + fentanyl IV) - patient sleepy but breathing independently, OR general anesthesia if patient prefers (fully asleep)
Explains local anesthesia: Throat and airways sprayed with local anesthetic (lignocaine) to suppress cough reflex and improve comfort
Describes biopsy technique: Small samples (biopsies) taken from lung mass using forceps passed through bronchoscope
Describes EBUS-TBNA: Ultrasound probe on bronchoscope tip visualizes lymph nodes, needle passed through airway wall to sample nodes (transbronchial needle aspiration)
Explains duration: Procedure takes 30-45 minutes, plus 1-2 hours recovery (total 2-3 hours in hospital)
Discusses common side effects: Sore throat (2-3 days), hoarse voice (temporary), cough (few days), blood-tinged sputum (small amount normal for 24 hours)
Discusses serious complications: Bleeding (1-2% risk, higher with biopsies), pneumothorax (1-2% risk if transbronchial biopsies), respiratory depression from sedation (<1%), infection (<1%)
Quantifies bleeding risk: Minor bleeding common (blood-tinged sputum), significant bleeding rare (<1%), massive bleeding very rare (<0.1%)
Addresses warfarin: INR 2.4 is ELEVATED for bronchoscopy with biopsies (target INR <1.5 for endobronchial biopsies, <1.2 for TBNA per BTS guidelines)

Plans warfarin management: STOP warfarin 5 days pre-procedure, check INR day before (target <1.5), bridge with LMWH if CHA₂DS₂-VASc high (patient has AF + age 65 = score 2, moderate risk - bridging recommended)
Explains bridging: LMWH (enoxaparin) injections subcutaneous while warfarin held, last dose 24 hours pre-procedure, restart warfarin evening of procedure
Advises NBM (nil by mouth): Nothing to eat 6 hours pre-procedure, sips water until 2 hours before (aspiration risk during sedation)
Arranges escort: Patient MUST have responsible adult to take home (cannot drive or operate machinery for 24 hours post-sedation)
Post-procedure instructions: No eating/drinking for 2 hours (until throat sensation returns), avoid hot liquids for 24 hours, no driving for 24 hours
Safety-netting post-procedure: Return immediately if: Significant haemoptysis (>2 tablespoons blood), chest pain, severe dyspnoea, fever >38°C
Discusses biopsy results timeline: Preliminary pathology 2-3 days, full report (including molecular testing if cancer) 7-10 days, follow-up appointment scheduled
Addresses loose teeth concern: Explains bronchoscope will be inserted carefully to avoid dislodging teeth, but dental trauma possible (rare, <0.1%)
Obtains informed consent: Checks patient understanding ('Can you tell me in your own words what the procedure involves?'), answers questions, confirms patient willing to proceed
Communicates empathetically, acknowledges anxiety, reassures about safety (common procedure, performed regularly, experienced team)
Documents consent: Completes written consent form, includes discussion of risks, confirms patient capacity to consent

osces.clinical_context: Bronchoscopy is the most common procedure in respiratory medicine, performed for diagnostic (tissue sampling, BAL) and therapeutic (foreign body removal, stent insertion) indications. Flexible bronchoscopy via transnasal or transoral route under conscious sedation (midazolam + fentanyl) is standard. EBUS-TBNA (endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration) allows real-time ultrasound-guided sampling of mediastinal lymph nodes via bronchoscope, replacing surgical mediastinoscopy in most cases (sensitivity ~90% for N2 staging). Complications: bleeding 1-2%, pneumothorax 1-2% (higher with transbronchial biopsies), respiratory depression <1%. Anticoagulation requires careful management: stop warfarin 5 days pre-procedure (target INR <1.5 for endobronchial biopsies), bridging LMWH if high thrombotic risk. Australian guidelines (TSANZ/BTS) recommend INR <1.2 for TBNA due to higher bleeding risk.
osces.examiner_notes: Assess candidate's ability to explain complex procedure using lay terminology and obtain valid informed consent. Strong candidates will describe bronchoscopy step-by-step (sedation, local anesthetic, bronchoscope insertion, biopsy, EBUS-TBNA) in patient-friendly language. Evaluate understanding of complication risks (bleeding 1-2%, pneumothorax 1-2%) and ability to quantify these to patient. Critical assessment point: warfarin management - candidates MUST recognize INR 2.4 is too high for bronchoscopy with biopsies and plan appropriate warfarin cessation + LMWH bridging (AF patient with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 requires bridging). Strong candidates will provide comprehensive pre-procedure instructions (NBM, escort required, medication adjustments) and post-procedure safety-netting. Communication skills paramount - obtaining informed consent requires checking patient understanding, answering questions, and respecting autonomy.

red_flags.flag: Massive haemoptysis post-bronchoscopy (>50mL bright red blood)
red_flags.action: Position patient bleeding side down, 100% oxygen, urgent CT chest, interventional radiology for bronchial artery embolization, thoracic surgery consult

red_flags.flag: Pneumothorax post-bronchoscopy (sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, absent breath sounds)
red_flags.action: Urgent CXR, if tension pneumothorax → immediate needle decompression (2nd ICS MCL), chest tube insertion

red_flags.flag: Respiratory depression during sedation (SpO2 <85%, apnoeic)
red_flags.action: Airway support (jaw thrust, bag-mask ventilation), reverse sedation (flumazenil for midazolam, naloxone for fentanyl), consider endotracheal intubation

red_flags.flag: Laryngospasm during bronchoscopy (stridor, unable to ventilate)
red_flags.action: Remove bronchoscope, 100% oxygen, positive pressure ventilation, if refractory → small dose propofol or suxamethonium + intubation

differential_diagnosis: Not applicable (bronchoscopy is diagnostic procedure, not diagnosis)

Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand (TSANZ) Guidelines for Bronchoscopy

Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists (ANZCA) Guidelines for Procedural Sedation
Yarmus L, Feller-Kopman D. Bronchoscopy for lung cancer staging. Curr Opin Pulm Med 2014; 20(4):321-326
